newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis, Palestinians clash over Jewish settlers.
newsitem.headline: Israelis, Palestinians clash over Jewish settlers.

text.p: Israeli soldiers fired rubber bullets and teargas on Thursday at Palestinians protesting against Israeli settlement in Jerusalem where Jews moved into another Arab neighbourhood.

One protester was taken to hospital with a rubber bullet wound and 13 were treated for teargas inhalation after clashes on the outskirts of Bethlehem, southeast of Jerusalem, a hospital official said.
In Gaza, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat compared Israel's settlement building in Arab East Jerusalem to "terrorism" and said it threatened to plunge the Middle East into violence.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu offered to finish making peace in six months but Palestinians called this a "publicity stunt" to avoid world condemnation for starting a settlement this week on a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
Israel has been on alert for a Palestinian backlash to the building at Jabal Abu Ghneim (Har Homa in Hebrew) but Arafat has ordered his police to restrain demonstrations.

Scores of youths, however, broke through police lines to hurl stones at the Israelis guarding the tomb of the biblical Rachel north of Bethlehem. The Israeli army said protesters hurled four firebombs at the troops but no one was hurt.
Bulldozers dug for a third day at Jabal Abu Ghneim while five settler families moved under cover of darkness into a sprawling house in the Arab Silwan neighbourhood.

Since 1991 at least 18 settler families have moved into Silwan, home to 30,000 Palestinians, an area just below the Old City walls where they say the biblical King David had the first capital of the Jewish people.
"This whole hill is part of ancient Jerusalem and our organisation's goal is for the whole hill to become Jewish," said Yigal Canaan, a spokesman for the El Ad settlers group.

Netanyahu's office said a settler leader had informed him of the entry into Silwan on Thursday but an official statement said the government did not initiate the action. Settlers said they had told Netanyahu the house was acquired legally.

A spokesman for the National Religious Party, the government's biggest champion of settlements, denied any significance to the timing so soon after the world condemned the groundbreaking for the 6,500-unit Jabal Abu Ghneim project.
Israel occupied East Jerusalem and the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East War. Palestinians regard East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state and consider the settlers a provocation.
Arafat accused Israel of "arrogance" by sidelining peace deals and ignoring international opinion.

"The continuation of this irresponsible Israeli position threatens to destroy and undermine the whole peace process and endangers order and security in the region and returns it to the cycle of violence and destruction," Arafat told Palestinian legislators.

Israeli security officials had predicted unrest following the groundbreaking on Tuesday, and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said army intelligence suggested the Palestinians would turn to violence during weekly Friday prayers.

Aides to Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat slammed the offer by Netanyahu, which emerged on Wednesday, to accelerate peace moves and called it a trick aimed at scrapping existing deals that call for three West Bank withdrawals of Israeli troops.
"We are speaking of a publicity stunt," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israel Radio. "This is a strategic proposal whose aim is to wipe out the interim agreement completely."
Arafat, who had appealed to Palestinians to shun violence, left Gaza for Cairo on Thursday for talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on the crisis.
Mubarak was anchoring crisis talks also with Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara and Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.

In Lebanon, Israeli jets hit Hizbollah guerrilla targets deep in northeast Lebanon near the Syrian border on Thursday, in apparent retaliation for the killing of an Israeli soldier by the guerrillas, security sources said.

Hizbollah (Party of God) swiftly said after the raid that it would step up its attacks in south Lebanon where Israeli troops occupy a 15 km (nine miles) deep zone to ward off guerrilla attacks on northern Israel.
